subtype: Approach: emotion-aware planning of the first weeks [Thinking]
passage: Lalremsiami, you asked how I got through the first weeks, so I'm Reena, and here is what I did. On the second night I sat on the floor and said out loud: these weeks will be heavy. That's normal. I won't fight it, I'll plan around it. I made a small list on the fridge. Go to class, even if I sit at the back. Eat three times, even if it's toast. Sleep by eleven, phone in the other room. And one rule: no big decisions on days when I'm crying. No changing courses, no messages to him, no cutting my hair. I wrote "ask again in two weeks" beside each idea. Some days I only managed the toast. But the list held the shape of the day while I could not.

qa.q: What time did Reena set for going to sleep?
qa.a: Reena set sleep by eleven.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling on the second night?
qa.a: Reena felt heavy and sad but accepting, saying the weeks would be hard and choosing to plan around them.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Reena add, and why?
qa.a: Reena could tell one close friend about the list so that someone checks in, because routines are easier to keep when another person knows about them.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Reena's account?
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked how Reena managed and receives a plain list, so Lalremsiami can see that getting through was about small steady steps and not a big recovery.

grounding: Shows planning around expected heavy weeks after a breakup by keeping classes, meals and sleep steady and postponing large choices.

subtype: Approach: leaning on friends and family [Action]
passage:
Sunday. Arohi told her two closest friends what had happened, over tea in the corridor. Neither tried to fix it. One said, "Come to the canteen tomorrow." Arohi did not want to go, but she went, and sat quiet while they talked about a film.
Wednesday. An invitation to a birthday dinner came. She almost said no. She wrote "yes" and went, and left early, and no one minded. That night, she phoned her sister Ritu, as she now did every week.
Saturday. Ritu said, "You sound less flat." Arohi noticed it too. The week had not been good, but it had not been lonely, and that was a different kind of hard.

qa.q: Which day did Arohi phone her sister Ritu?
qa.a: Arohi phoned her sister Ritu on Wednesday night.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel when the birthday dinner invitation came?
qa.a: Arohi almost said no, so she felt reluctant and unwilling, but she chose to go anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Arohi add, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could plan one small activity she used to enjoy, because company helps but a familiar activity can also bring back some ease.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Arohi's week?
qa.a: Ritu hears the weekly call and says Arohi sounds less flat, so Ritu can tell from her voice that the support is helping a little.

grounding: Shows leaning on friends and family after a breakup by talking, accepting invitations even when unwilling, and a weekly call.

subtype: Approach: checking the ex's profiles repeatedly [Pitfall]
passage: At the tram stop in Seoul, Jin took out his phone and opened his ex's page, again. Nothing new. He scrolled to a photo from three weeks earlier and stared. Was she smiling at the camera or at someone? He checked who had liked it. He put the phone away, then took it out again. By the time the tram came, his chest felt as tight as it had on the first day. Paulo, his classmate, sat down beside him. "You've been on that page for a month," said Paulo quietly. "I know." "Does it help?" Jin looked at the phone and did not answer. It had been six weeks, and each glance had made the breakup feel as fresh as the day it happened.

qa.q: At which kind of place was Jin looking at his phone?
qa.a: Jin was at the tram stop in Seoul.

qa.q: What is Jin feeling as he stares at the photo?
qa.a: Jin feels hurt and hopeful at once, searching for a sign in the smile and finding his chest tight again.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Jin use instead of checking, and why?
qa.a: Jin could mute the page and keep his phone in a bag during commutes, because fewer glances would give the hurt fewer chances to reopen.

qa.q: How does Paulo see Jin's habit?
qa.a: Paulo has watched Jin on that page for a month and asks gently if it helps, so Paulo sees a friend hurting himself with each glance.

grounding: Shows repeatedly checking an ex's posts for a sign, which reopens the hurt and keeps the breakup fresh long after it ended.

subtype: Approach: reducing triggers by muting and removing reminders [Action]
passage: Chaitanya, you asked what actually helped, so I'm Ujjwal and I'll be practical. I did three small things in one afternoon. First, I muted her accounts. Not blocked, not an announcement, just quiet. I did not want a scene. Second, I moved all our photos into a folder called "later", not deleted, just out of sight. Third, my usual route to class went past her department, so I started walking around by the library. It added six minutes. No one knew, and I did not tell anyone. It felt slightly silly, like arranging a room so you don't keep bumping into the same chair. But my mornings stopped starting with a jab. Space to heal, I found, is mostly not seeing things.

qa.q: How many extra minutes did the new route to class add?
qa.a: The new route added six minutes.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling about the changes while making them?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt a little silly but determined, comparing it to moving a room so that a chair is not bumped again.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ujjwal add, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal could plan something to do in the time that used to go into checking, because removing reminders leaves a gap that something else should fill.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Ujjwal's steps?
qa.a: Chaitanya asked what helped and hears three practical steps with no scene, so Chaitanya sees a plan that anyone could copy quietly.

grounding: Shows muting accounts, storing old photos out of sight and changing a route to reduce reminders after a breakup, without any confrontation.

subtype: Approach: rebound relationship to avoid the feeling [Pitfall]
passage:
Chinmay: I'm seeing someone
Nikita: Already? It's been 4 days
Chinmay: I know. We met at the fest. She's fun. I'm not thinking about anything else
Nikita: Are you okay?
Chinmay: Yes. Busy. That's the point
Chinmay: Three weeks later
Chinmay: It's over. She said I was somewhere else the whole time
Nikita: What do you think?
Chinmay: She's right. Every time we were quiet I was thinking about the breakup. I used her to not feel it
Nikita: That sounds like it hurts
Chinmay: Both of us. I feel bad for her. And the sadness is exactly where I left it
Nikita: Do you want to talk about it properly?
Chinmay: Yes. This time yes

qa.q: How many days after the breakup did Chinmay start seeing someone?
qa.a: It had been 4 days.

qa.q: What is Chinmay feeling at the end of the chat?
qa.a: Chinmay feels sad and guilty, regretting using the new partner to avoid the feeling and admitting the sadness is exactly where it was left.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chinmay have used, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could have given the grief some quiet time and leaned on friends like Nikita, because a new relationship can cover pain but does not face it.

qa.q: How might the new partner have felt when the relationship ended?
qa.a: The new partner said Chinmay was somewhere else the whole time, so the partner probably felt unseen and hurt.

grounding: Shows starting a new relationship within days to escape loneliness, and its ending because the grief was never faced.

passage: On Monday evening in the campus sports hall, Anand signed up for the gym, and the instructor, Thomas, handed him a card. "What are you working towards?" "Nothing exactly," said Anand. "Just, being busy." Thomas nodded. "Busy works. Come three times a week." On the way out, Anand stopped at the notice board and paid the fee for a weekend class in web design. That night, he opened a laptop and started a small project: a page listing the hostel's laundry timings. By the third week he had a routine: gym at six, class on Saturday, code every night for an hour. The evenings were full. On Sunday his page went live, and three people used it, which felt like a small win.

qa.q: How often did Thomas tell Anand to come to the gym?
qa.a: Thomas told Anand to come three times a week.

qa.q: What is Anand feeling when he says he is working towards nothing exactly?
qa.a: Anand feels empty and restless, wanting to be busy without a clear goal, though he gradually finds small wins.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anand add, and why?
qa.a: Anand could also spend time with friends and tell them how he is feeling, because a full schedule builds confidence but does not replace talking.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Anand's answer?
qa.a: Thomas nods and accepts that busy can work for now, so Thomas treats the plan as a starting point, not a problem.

grounding: Shows channelling post-breakup energy into fitness, a small coding project and a class so that evenings fill with small wins.

subtype: Approach: reflecting on what was learned [Thinking]
passage:
Week two. Farhan sat with his friend Vijay on the terrace and said, "I keep having the same thoughts." "Then write them down," Vijay said. Farhan didn't.
Week six. On a slow Sunday he took out a notebook and made three headings. What I valued: she listened, and she was funny. What didn't work: we avoided arguments and let things pile up. What I want next time: someone who can talk about small annoyances early, and me, learning to say them. He wrote slowly, sometimes staring at the wall.
Week eight. Vijay asked, "Are you still stuck?" Farhan smiled, a little. "Not stuck. Clearer." He showed Vijay the page.

qa.q: On which week did Farhan take out the notebook?
qa.a: Farhan took out the notebook in week six.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling at week eight when he shows the page?
qa.a: Farhan feels a quiet clarity and a small smile of relief, saying he is not stuck but clearer.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Farhan add, and why?
qa.a: Farhan could talk it through with a trusted friend as well, because writing sorts thoughts while talking may show a view he cannot see alone.

qa.q: How does Vijay see Farhan's change?
qa.a: Vijay first suggests writing and later asks if Farhan is still stuck, so Vijay watches patiently and is invited to read the page at the end.

grounding: Shows reflecting after some weeks on what was valued, what failed and what is wanted next time, turning pain into clearer ideas about partners.

passage: I share a hostel room with Uday, so I know his nights. For about three weeks after the breakup, he lay awake with the lamp off but his eyes open. Once around two, he said into the dark, half to himself, "If I had just said sorry that Friday." Another night: "If I hadn't brought up her friend." He would go over one conversation, then another, changing one sentence each time, and the ending never changed. In the mornings he came to class with red eyes and forgot what the professor said. I don't know exactly what he felt. Once I made him tea at three and said nothing. He drank it and said, "Thanks. It never works, does it?" — Pradeep

qa.q: What time did Uday say something into the dark once?
qa.a: Uday spoke around two.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt during those nights, according to what Pradeep saw?
qa.a: Uday may have felt regret and helplessness, going over the conversations and hoping for a different ending, though Pradeep says the exact feeling cannot be known.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Uday try at night, and why?
qa.a: Uday could write the thoughts on paper and close the notebook, or talk to someone in the daytime, because replaying does not change the past and paper or a person gives the thoughts somewhere to go.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep to watch Uday in the dark room?
qa.a: Pradeep can only hear and guess, so Pradeep makes tea and stays quiet, since Pradeep does not want to claim to know what Uday feels.

grounding: Shows nightly replaying of old conversations to find what could have been changed, costing sleep and concentration.

subtype: Approach: seeking professional support when low persists [Revision]
passage: Three months after the breakup, Jana noticed she was still not sleeping through the night, and her seminar notes had gone blank for weeks. For two months a heaviness had followed her from class to the library and back. Her flatmate Jamal said one evening, "It's been long. Maybe someone could help?" Jana had been telling herself to wait. This time she opened the university's website, found the counselling page and picked a time for Thursday. The counsellor in a small warm room did not hurry her. "It's good you came," they said. "Tell me what the last two months have been like." She talked for forty minutes. Walking out, she felt lighter, like someone had shared the weight.

qa.q: On which day did Jana book the counselling visit?
qa.a: Jana booked the visit for Thursday.

qa.q: What is Jana feeling as she leaves the counsellor's room?
qa.a: Jana feels lighter and supported, as though someone has shared the weight.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Jana add, and why?
qa.a: Jana could keep a few regular habits, such as meals and a short walk, because support from a counsellor works best alongside small steady routines.

qa.q: How might Jamal see Jana's decision?
qa.a: Jamal saw the long low stretch and gently suggested help, so Jamal is probably relieved that Jana acted instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows booking a campus counsellor visit when sadness stays heavy and affects study, instead of waiting longer.

subtype: Approach: revising the plan after a setback [Revision]
passage: Counsellor's note, written by Rukmini. Parul came in on Tuesday, a little shaken. At the college fest on Saturday, Parul had seen the ex across the courtyard, felt a hot rush to the face, and left early. Parul's first sentence was "I thought I was past this. I'm back to zero." I asked what a friend would say. Parul paused. "That one bad moment is not zero." We then planned, not to avoid the ex, but to be ready. A calm exit line: "Good to see you, I have to go." A friend nearby at any big event. A ten-minute walk after. Parul wrote them on a card. I only asked one question: "What would help you most?" The plan was Parul's, not mine.

qa.q: What was Parul's calm exit line?
qa.a: Parul's exit line was 'Good to see you, I have to go.'

qa.q: How did Parul feel after seeing the ex at the fest?
qa.a: Parul felt shaken, with a hot rush to the face, and worried about being back to zero.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Parul add, and why?
qa.a: Parul could arrange to meet a friend before an event where the ex may be present, because company gives a safer place to breathe and leave.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Parul's response?
qa.a: Rukmini watches Parul decide the plan alone after one question, so Rukmini sees someone who treats a bad moment as a signal and not a failure.

grounding: Shows revising a plan after an unexpected encounter with an ex, treating it as a signal and preparing a calm exit line and a friend nearby.
